newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcies soar as economic recovery slow.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcies soar as economic recovery slow.

text.p: The number of bankruptcies jumped 10 percent last month as Corporate Japan continues to suffer from the nation's deep-seated economic problems, a report said Friday.

Private credit research agency Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd. said the number of bankruptcies rose nearly 10 percent to 1,236 from January 1996. It was the 48th month in a row the number of bankruptcies has exceeded 1,000.
Total debts held by businesses that went bust in January more than doubled, as firms sank under the weight of debts left over from the free-wheeling economic growth of the 1980s, Tokyo Shoko said.
Bankruptcies increased in all industry sectors except for the retail and service sectors and a total of 14,524 Japanese workers lost their jobs because of the failures.
The credit research company said that for the first time mid-level companies, "exhausted by prolonged economic sluggishness," have started failing in larger numbers.

The January bankruptcies included that of Kyotaru Co. Ltd., a sushi restaurant chain with estimated debts of 101.3 billion yen ($810 million). Kyotaru was the first company listed on the main section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange to fail since mid-1993.

The failure was taken as a sign that Corporate Japan remained in deep trouble, and analysts said the number of bankruptcies would remain high and the outlook bleak as the economy continues to struggle.
Also in January, Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten, a diamond and jewelry company, went bankrupt with debts of 60 billion yen ($480 million).
Financial firms Sanwa Tatemono Sogo Finance Co. Ltd. and CS Sogo Service Kabushiki Kaisha also failed.
All four firms suffered as a result of aggressive business practices during the 1980s.
About 60 percent of bankruptcies in January resulted from factors which Tokyo Shoko said were typical of a slow economy, sluggish sales, accumulated losses and unpaid bills.
